title: Fast and slow pointers
objectives: Detect a cycle in a linked list with two pointers.
Find the middle node of a list in one pass
Explain why resetting one pointer to the head finds the start of the cycle

screens.title: A list with no end
screens.prose: A walk `cur = cur.next` normally stops at `None`. In this list the last node, 6, points back to an earlier node instead.

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

state.caption: Start at the head and follow the arrows

screens.question: Following the arrows from the head, tap the first node you reach for a second time.

hints.text: Walk it out: 1, 2, 3, … Where does 6 lead?
The last node points back here.
The walk goes 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and then back to 3. So 3 is the first node you meet twice.

feedback.correct: 6 leads back to 3, and the walk goes round 3, 4, 5, 6 for ever.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow each arrow in turn until a node repeats.

byKey.n1: Nothing points back to 1. The walk never returns to the head.
byKey.n6: 6 is the last new node. Its arrow leads back to an earlier one.
byKey.n4: 4 does repeat, but 3 comes round first.

explain.text: After 6 the walk returns to 3, so `cur` is never `None`. The list has a **cycle** of four nodes, 3 to 6, and a loop over it never ends. We want to detect that.

screens.title: Remember everything
screens.prose:
One fix is to remember every node seen:

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    seen = set()
    cur = head
    while cur:
        if cur in seen:
            return True
        seen.add(cur)
        cur = cur.next
    return False
```

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

screens.question: How many nodes are in `seen` when it returns `True` on this list?

widget.label: Nodes in seen
widget.accept: 6: every node, before 3 comes round again

hints.text: When does `cur in seen` first become true?
3 is the first repeated node, reached after 6.
Nodes 1 to 6 are added one by one. Then `cur` is 3 again, already in `seen`. So `seen` holds 6 nodes.

feedback.correct: All 6 nodes are stored before 3 repeats.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the nodes added before the first repeat.

byKey.cycle: The tail nodes 1 and 2 are added too.
byKey.seven: When 3 comes round again it is found in `seen` and not added a second time.
byKey.three: The walk passes 4, 5 and 6 before it returns to 3.

explain.text: `seen` grows with every node, so the memory is $O(n)$. It is correct and simple to write. The question that follows is: can we do it in $O(1)$ extra space?

screens.title: Two speeds
screens.prose: Another way needs only two names. `slow` moves one node per move; `fast` moves two. If the list ends, `fast` reaches `None` first. If there is a cycle, `fast` keeps going round.

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

screens.question: Step both pointers until you can say whether there is a cycle.

ops.label: Stop: they are on the same node
ops.why: They start together at the head. Look for a meeting only after a move.

ops.label: Move both 1 step
ops.why: At the same speed the gap between them never changes, so they would never meet.

ops.label: Stop: no cycle
ops.why: `fast` has not reached `None`, so the list has not ended. Keep moving.

ops.label: Stop: `fast` is behind `slow`, so something is wrong
ops.why: `fast` is behind only because it went round the cycle. It is now closing in from behind.

ops.label: They meet: there is a cycle
Move: `slow` 1 step, `fast` 2 steps
ops.why: They are on the same node. That meeting proves the cycle; stop here.

hints.text: After each move, are they on the same node?
`fast` enters the cycle first and goes round it.
Positions after each move: (2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 3), (5, 5). They meet at 5 after four moves.

feedback.correct: `fast` lapped the cycle and caught `slow` at node 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep moving `slow` 1 and `fast` 2 until they share a node.

explain.text: Inside the cycle `fast` gains one node per move, so it must land on `slow` rather than jump over it. This is **Floyd's cycle detection**, or the tortoise and the hare. It uses two names: $O(1)$ extra space.

screens.title: Why they must meet
screens.prose: When `slow` first reaches node 3, the start of the cycle, `fast` is at node 5. The cycle has 4 nodes. Each move, `fast` gains exactly one node on `slow`.

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

state.caption: `fast` is 2 nodes ahead along the cycle, so 2 behind

screens.question: How many more moves until they meet?

widget.label: Moves
widget.accept: 2: `fast` is 2 nodes behind round the cycle and gains 1 per move

hints.text: Going round the cycle from 5, how far is it to 3?
From 5 the cycle runs 6, then back to 3.
`fast` is 2 nodes behind `slow` along the cycle. Gaining 1 per move, it catches up in 2 moves.

feedback.correct: A gap of 2 closes at 1 per move: 2 moves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Measure how far `fast` is behind `slow`, going forwards round the cycle.

byKey.lap: That is the cycle's length. The gap is only 2, and it shrinks by 1 each move.
byKey.one: After one move `slow` is at 4 and `fast` at 3. They are not together yet.

explain.text: The gap behind `slow` goes 2, then 1, then 0. It never skips 0, because it shrinks by exactly one. So once `slow` is in a cycle of length $L$, they meet within $L$ moves: $O(n)$ in all.

screens.title: The middle in one pass
screens.prose:
With no cycle, the same two speeds find the middle. `fast` covers the list twice as quickly, so when it runs out, `slow` is halfway.

```python
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
```

params.aria: A linked list with no cycle

screens.question: Tap the node where `slow` stops.

hints.text: Where are `slow` and `fast` after each pass of the loop?
After two passes `slow` is on 30 and `fast` on 50.
Pass 1: 20 and 30. Pass 2: 30 and 50. Pass 3: 40 and `None`, since 50's next is 60 and 60's next is `None`. The loop stops with `slow` on 40.

feedback.correct: `slow` stops on 40, the second of the two middle nodes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the loop pass by pass, checking the condition each time.

byKey.m2: 30 is the first middle. With 50 not the last node, the loop runs a third time and `slow` moves to 40.
byKey.m4: `slow` moves one node per pass, and the loop runs three times.

explain.text: With an even count there are two middles, and this loop returns the second, 40. With 5 nodes it returns the 3rd; with 2 nodes, the 2nd; with 1, the only one. An empty list skips the loop and returns `None`.

screens.title: The order of the checks
screens.prose:
A first attempt at `has_cycle`:

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            return True
    return False
```

params.aria: A linked list with no cycle

screens.question: What does `has_cycle(from_list([1, 2]))` do?

options.why: You expected `and` to test `fast` first. It runs left to right, so `fast.next` is read while `fast` is `None`.
`slow` is node 2 and `fast` is `None` after one pass, so `slow is fast` is false.
There is no cycle, and the next condition check fails at once.

hints.text: After the first pass, what is `fast`?
`fast` jumps from 1 past 2 to the `None` after it.
After one pass `fast` is `None`. The condition then evaluates `fast.next` first, which raises before `and fast` is reached.

feedback.correct: `fast.next` on `None` raises before the `fast` check is reached.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run one pass, then evaluate the condition left to right.

byKey.b: You read the condition as if `fast` were checked first. `and` runs left to right, so `fast.next` comes first.

explain.text: After one pass `fast` is `None`, and the condition reads `None.next`. Write `while fast and fast.next:`: if `fast` is `None`, `and` stops before reading `.next`. The same order also handles an empty list.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
Two pointers at different speeds:

```python
slow = fast = head
while fast and fast.next:
    slow = slow.next
    fast = fast.next.next
    if slow is fast:
        return True   # a cycle
return False          # fast reached the end
```

No cycle: `fast` reaches the end and `slow` is at the middle. A cycle: they meet within $L$ moves of `slow` entering it.
screens.question: Why can `fast` never jump over `slow` inside the cycle?

options.text: Each move closes the gap between them by exactly one node
`fast` moves two nodes, so it lands on every node
options.why: `fast` skips every other node. What matters is the gap, which shrinks by exactly one.

options.text: The cycle always has an even length
options.why: The cycle can have any length. The argument works for all of them.
Both keep moving. `fast` gains one node per move.

feedback.correct: A gap that shrinks by one each move must reach 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. How does the distance from `fast` to `slow` change on each move?

explain.text: `fast` moves 2 and `slow` moves 1, so the gap changes by $2 - 1 = 1$. Counting down by one from any start, it hits 0 exactly. A speed of 3 against 1 could skip over 0.

screens.title: Write both
screens.prose: The prelude adds `make_cycle(values, pos)`: it builds the list, then points the tail back at index `pos`. So `make_cycle([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], 2)` is the list from this lesson. Aim for $O(1)$ space: two tests check your peak memory.

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

screens.question: Write `has_cycle(head)` and `middle(head)`; for an even count, `middle` returns the second middle node.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests. They try an empty list (`None`), a self-loop, two nodes with and without a cycle, and 100,000 nodes. `middle` returns the node; the tests read its `.val`. Tests 13 and 14 check the peak memory of each function on 100,000 nodes.

hints.text: Both functions use the same loop. What differs?
Check `fast` before `fast.next`, every time round.
Both: `slow = fast = head`, `while fast and fast.next:` move `slow` 1 and `fast` 2. `has_cycle` returns `True` when `slow is fast`, else `False`. `middle` returns `slow`.

feedback.correct: One loop shape, two answers: a meeting, or the middle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 passes `None`. `while fast and fast.next:` skips the loop when `fast` is `None`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 has two nodes and no cycle. An `AttributeError` means `fast.next` was read while `fast` was `None`.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is one node pointing to itself. After one move both pointers are on it, so `slow is fast`.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 has six nodes and expects 40, the second middle. Loop while `fast and fast.next`.

explain.text: Compare nodes with `is`, not values with `==`: two nodes can hold the same value. A self-loop is caught after one move. Both functions are $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

screens.title: Where the cycle starts
screens.prose: Let $a$ be the steps from the head to the cycle's start. Let $b$ be the steps on to the meeting point, and $L$ the cycle's length. In our list $a = 2$, $b = 2$ and $L = 4$. Order the argument for finding the start.

params.aria: A linked list whose tail points back into the middle

screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: At the meeting, `slow` has taken $a + b$ steps
`fast` has taken $2(a + b)$; the extra $a + b$ is whole laps, so $a + b = kL$
So $a = kL - b$: from the meeting point, $a$ steps forward reach the start
Reset one pointer to the head and move both 1 step at a time; they meet at the start

hints.text: Which line is a fact about `slow` alone?
`slow` stands $b$ steps into the cycle.
Count `slow`'s steps, then `fast`'s. Their difference is whole laps. Solve for $a$, then use it to place both pointers.

feedback.correct: Steps, laps, solve for $a$, then walk $a$ steps from both ends.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from what each pointer has walked, then compare them.

byKey.reset: The reset is the algorithm. It comes last, once $a = kL - b$ says why it works.

explain.text: Here $a + b = 4 = 1 \times L$, so $k = 1$. From the meeting point 5, $a = 2$ steps go 6, then 3; from the head, 2 steps go 2, then 3. Both arrive at 3, the start of the cycle.

canvas.caption: Head and meeting point are both 2 steps from node 3

screens.title: A pricing-rule chain
screens.prose: A pricing system falls back from rule to rule. `fallback` maps each rule to the next one, or to `None`; a rule missing from the dict has no fallback. A bad edit can create a loop, and the pricer then hangs. Check a chain without storing it.

params.aria: Pricing rules p, q, r, s with a loop q to r to s to q

screens.question: Write `has_loop(fallback, start)`: `True` if following fallbacks from `start` never ends, using $O(1)$ extra space.

widget.prelude:
import tracemalloc as _tm
def peak_bytes(f):
    _tm.start()
    try:
        f()
        return _tm.get_traced_memory()[1]
    finally:
        _tm.stop()
widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests. They include a chain ending in `None`, a rule pointing to itself, an empty dict and a missing rule. Test 8 is a chain of 100,000 rules that loops, and test 9 checks your peak memory on it.

hints.text: What plays the part of `.next` here?
`fallback.get(rule)` gives the next rule, or `None` when there is none.

Loop `while fast is not None and fallback.get(fast) is not None:`. Move `slow = fallback.get(slow)` and `fast = fallback.get(fallback.get(fast))`. Return `True` when `fast` is not `None` and they are equal; else `False` after the loop.

feedback.correct: Floyd's method works on any chain where each item names the next.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 is a rule that falls back to itself. After one move both pointers are on it.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 has an empty dict. Use `fallback.get(fast)` so a missing rule counts as `None`, not a `KeyError`.
byKey.test-5: Test 5: `"y"` is not in the dict, so the chain ends there. Use `.get` for both of `fast`'s steps, so a missing rule gives `None`.

explain.text: `fallback[x]` plays the part of `x.next`, and a missing key plays `None`. Rule names are strings, so `==` compares them. The check needs two names, however long the chain.

ideas: Move `slow` one step and `fast` two. Without a cycle, `fast` reaches the end and `slow` is at the middle.
With a cycle, the gap shrinks by one node per move, so they meet within one lap. That is $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.
After they meet, start one pointer at the head and one at the meeting point. Moving one step each, they meet at the cycle's start.

formula.name: Floyd's cycle start
formula.tex: a + b = kL \;\Rightarrow\; a = kL - b
formula.note: $a$: head to cycle start; $b$: start to meeting point; $L$: cycle length.

summary.trap: `while fast.next and fast` reads `.next` from `None` at the end of a list. Test `fast` first: `while fast and fast.next`.

quiz.prose: A single node whose `next` is itself: `n = Node(5); n.next = n`.
quiz.question: What does `has_cycle(n)` return?

options.why: `n.next` is `n`, not `None`, so the loop runs, and after one move both pointers are on `n`.
Nothing here is `None`: every `.next` leads back to `n`.

feedback.correct: A node pointing to itself is a cycle of length 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Where are both pointers after one move?

explain.text: `slow` moves to `n.next`, which is `n`; `fast` moves two steps, also to `n`. So `slow is fast` after one move, and it returns `True`.

quiz.prose: `middle` uses `while fast and fast.next:` and runs on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4.
quiz.question: Which node does it return?

options.why: That is the first middle. The loop runs twice here, so `slow` reaches 3.
`slow` moves once per pass and there are only two passes.

feedback.correct: Two passes put `slow` on 3, the second middle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the loop pass by pass.

explain.text: Pass 1: `slow` 2, `fast` 3. Pass 2: `slow` 3, `fast` `None`. The loop stops and returns 3.

quiz.prose: A chain of 10,000,000 linked records may contain a loop.
quiz.question: How much extra memory do the two approaches need?

options.text: A set of seen nodes: up to 10,000,000 entries; Floyd: two names

options.why: Floyd stores only `slow` and `fast`, whatever the length.
The set stores a reference to every node it passes.

options.text: Floyd needs more, because `fast` visits nodes twice
options.why: Visiting costs time, not memory. Floyd remembers nothing it has passed.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does each method have to remember?

explain.text: The set grows with every node, so it may hold all 10,000,000. Floyd keeps two references and still finishes in $O(n)$ time. That saving in memory is why Floyd's method is worth knowing.

quiz.prose: A tortoise and a hare start together on a 400 m circular track. The hare runs twice as fast. Neither stops.
quiz.question: How far has the tortoise run when the hare first catches it again?

widget.label: Distance
widget.accept: 400 m: the hare has run 800 m, one lap more

feedback.correct: The hare gains one full lap when the tortoise has run 400 m.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The hare must gain exactly one lap, 400 m.

byKey.hare: That is the hare's distance. The tortoise covers half of it.
byKey.half: At 200 m the hare has run 400 m: one lap, but the tortoise is not at the start.

explain.text: The hare gains as much ground as the tortoise covers. To lap it, the hare must gain 400 m, so the tortoise runs 400 m and the hare 800 m. In the list, the lap is the cycle and the gain is one node per move.
